Get started with WildObsR

Source: vignettes/WildObsR.Rmd
WildObsR.Rmd

WildObsR finds, downloads and prepares camera trap data from WildObs, Australia’s national wildlife camera database. Every project arrives as a Camera Trap Data Package (Camtrap DP), which contains tables of camera deployments, observations, media, and a WildObs-generated table containing spatio-temporal covariates for each camera deployment, along with the Creative Commons licences, formatted citation and field definitions that travel with the data package. This vignette takes you from installation to your first downloaded data package in about ten lines of code.

Install WildObsR

WildObsR is installed from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("WildObs/WildObsR")

remotes::install_github("WildObs/WildObsR") works too. WildObsR relies on the spatial package sf, which needs the GDAL, PROJ and GEOS libraries. On Windows and macOS they come with sf itself. On Linux, install them first, for example sudo apt install libgdal-dev libproj-dev libgeos-dev libssl-dev on Ubuntu.

To install a particular release rather than the latest version, add its tag, for example pak::pak("WildObs/WildObsR@v0.2.0").

Get an API key

Database access requires a personal API key, tied to your own WildObs account. API keys are generated per-user, not per-project. All API keys provides access to the public WildObs Database, where sensitive species records are obscured and data sharing agreements are applied. Therefore, each API key delivers the same data for everyone.

  1. Create an account or log in at the WildObs Dashboard.
    • Note that if you have submitted data to the WildObs Database, please create an account using the same email address you used to share data to ensure you have access to your private unobscured data.
  2. Under WildObs Database, select Get Started to open the database page.
  3. In the panel at the top right, select Create under API Key, and copy the key. Treat it like a password: do not share it or paste it into a script.
  4. Store it in your .Renviron file, which R reads when it starts, so the key stays out of your code. Open the file with usethis::edit_r_environ(), add the line below with your own key, save it and restart R.
WILDOBSR_API_KEY=your_key_here

Paste the key without quotes or spaces after the =, and end the file with a blank line, or R ignores the last entry. Then read the key into your session:

library(WildObsR)

# read the key from .Renviron; it is never printed
api_key <- Sys.getenv("WILDOBSR_API_KEY")
# Check that R has found it, should return TRUE 
nzchar(api_key)
#> [1] TRUE

If this returns FALSE, check the spelling of WILDOBSR_API_KEY and that you restarted your R session.

Find projects

wildobs_mongo_query() is a quick and light-weight function that queries the metadata of all projects along multiple parameters and returns the IDs of those that match. Filters include where in space camera were active, time surveys were collecting data, species detected in the survey, camera deployment sampling designs, and contributors associated with each project. Multiple filters can be combined, and the projects that are returned must match all of them. Here we look for projects in a spatial box around the Wet Tropics Rainforests of Far North Queensland that list Zachary Amir as a contributor:

# a box around the Wet Tropics, in latitude and longitude (i.e., decimal degrees)
wet_tropics <- list(xmin = 144.9, xmax = 146.5, ymin = -19.6, ymax = -15.3)

# find every project with cameras inside the box and Zachary Amir among its contributors
ids <- wildobs_mongo_query(api_key = api_key, spatial = wet_tropics,
                           contributors = "Zachary Amir")
# check which project IDs were returned
ids
#> [1] "ZAmir_QLD_Wet_Tropics_2022_WildObsID_0001"

Leave out contributors to see every project in the box.

By default the search returns two kinds of projects:

  • Open projects, which have no remaining embargo period, contain all available data tables.
    • Include tabularSharingPreference = "open" in wildobs_mongo_query() to find only projects you can download in full.
  • Partial projects have a remaining embargo period, and only contain their project-level metadata. This data is useful for discovering projects and providing information such as where, when and who collected the data.

You can learn more about WildObs’s data sharing agreements here.

Download them

wildobs_dp_download() returns a named list with one data package per project. Media tables, which record one row per camera trap image or video are by far the largest table, and the default behavior of this function is to leave it out unless you ask for media = TRUE.

# one data package per project, without the media table
dp_list <- wildobs_dp_download(api_key = api_key, project_ids = ids)

# count how many tables each package holds; a partial project holds none
vapply(dp_list, function(dp) length(dp$resources), integer(1))
#> ZAmir_QLD_Wet_Tropics_2022_WildObsID_0001 
#>                                         3

Each package holds its tables as Frictionless Data Package resources. Read them with frictionless::read_resource(), which returns each column with the type its schema defines, and formats date-times in the project’s own time zone. The package also keeps a copy in dp$data, because the camtrapdp class expects one, but other tools do not always keep that copy up to date, so read tables with read_resource().

# the first open project
dp <- dp_list[["ZAmir_QLD_Wet_Tropics_2022_WildObsID_0001"]] # or dp_list[[1]]

# read the camera deployments table, one row per camera deployment
deployments <- frictionless::read_resource(dp, "deployments")
# inspect a few key fields 
head(deployments[, c("deploymentID", "locationName", "deploymentStart", "deploymentEnd")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   deploymentID              locationName deploymentStart     deploymentEnd      
#>   <chr>                     <chr>        <dttm>              <dttm>             
#> 1 CFRAG_01_WildObsID_0001_… Eacham_Curt… 2022-12-15 08:52:45 2023-02-15 10:46:32
#> 2 CFRAG_01_WildObsID_0001_… Eacham_Curt… 2022-12-15 08:19:27 2023-03-06 13:29:49
#> 3 CFRAG_02_WildObsID_0001_… Eacham_Curt… 2022-12-15 09:58:36 2023-02-12 06:42:14
#> 4 CFRAG_02_WildObsID_0001_… Eacham_Curt… 2022-12-15 09:40:56 2023-03-07 14:11:01
#> 5 CFRAG_03_WildObsID_0001_… Eacham_Curt… 2022-12-15 11:00:58 2023-03-06 15:18:39
#> 6 CFRAG_03_WildObsID_0001_… Eacham_Curt… 2022-12-15 10:36:47 2023-03-03 23:08:06

# read the observations table
observations <- frictionless::read_resource(dp, "observations")
# inspect what types of observations are contained in this table 
sort(table(observations$observationType))
#> 
#> unclassified      unknown        human      vehicle       animal        blank 
#>            0            8        14832        16641        33522        65679

Set obscured records aside

Records of threatened species are obscured where the species is listed under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999. They keep the species, date and count, but the foreign keys that link back to both the deployments, media, and covariates tables read obscured_for_<category>_species, so they cannot be joined. Count them, then set them aside before any spatial analysis:

# which detections cannot be placed on a camera
obscured <- grepl("^obscured_for_", observations$deploymentID)
# how many, by threat category
table(observations$deploymentID[obscured])
#> 
#> obscured_for_endangered_species 
#>                             452
# keep the rest
observations <- observations[!obscured, ]

Read the metadata, and cite the data

extract_metadata() turns the metadata of one or many packages into tables, such as who collected the data, under which licence, and with what sampling design. cite_datapackages() provides citations formatted by WildObs, including each dataset’s Research Activity Identifier (RAiD), which provides a persistent identifier to reference data used in research. Additional parameters allow you to include the data package version you downloaded and citations for the WildObs-generated covariates table.

# the licence of every project
extract_metadata(dp_list, "licenses")[, c("name", "scope", "DPID")]
#>        name scope                                      DPID
#> 1 CC-BY-4.0  data ZAmir_QLD_Wet_Tropics_2022_WildObsID_0001
#> 2 CC-BY-4.0 media ZAmir_QLD_Wet_Tropics_2022_WildObsID_0001

# the references to cite, one per project
writeLines(cite_datapackages(dp_list))
#> Zachary Amir, Tom Bruce & Matthew Luskin (2022). WildObs Camera Trap Data Package: Zachary Amir's camera trap surveys from 6 national parks in QLD's Wet Tropics rainforests from late 2022 to early 2023 targeting feral and native vertebrates [Camera Trap Data Package]. WildObs National Wildlife Camera Database. https://wildobs.org.au. RAiD: https://raid.org/10.83062/cb5829ab. WildObs data package version 1.2.0.

Work offline with the example data

Two open projects ship with WildObsR, so you can try every function without a key or an internet connection. example_datapackages() returns them in the same shape as wildobs_dp_download(), with animal detections only and no media table:

# the bundled copies of two projects
examples <- example_datapackages()
names(examples)
#> [1] "ZAmir_QLD_Wet_Tropics_2022_WildObsID_0001"           
#> [2] "NSW_Woomargama_wombats_Linley_2021-22_WildObsID_0010"
